title: De Quantitate Animae
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa059.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Quod si te illud movet, quod solemus cam quant Graeci μαϰροθυμιαν vocant, longanimitatem inlerpretari; animadvertere licet a corpore ad animum multa verba transferri, sicut ab animo ad corpus: nam si montem improbum, et justissimam tellurem dixit Virgilius (Æneid. lib. 12, I. 687; Georg. lib. 2, I. 460), quae verba cernis ab animo ad corpora esse translata; quid mirum si mutua vice longanimitatem dicimus, cam longa nisi corpora esse non possint? Ea vero inter virr tutes quæ appellatur animi magnitudo, ad nullum spatium, sed ad vim quamdam, id est ad potestatem potentiamque animi relata recte inteNigilnr;
passages.english: But if you are troubled by the fact that we usually render what the Greeks call *makrothymia* as "longanimity" [long-suffering], you may notice that many words are transferred from the body to the mind, just as from the mind to the body. For if Virgil spoke of a "wicked mountain" and "most just earth" (Aeneid 12.687; Georgics 2.460), words which you see have been transferred from the mind to bodies, what wonder is it if we, in the opposite direction, say "longanimity", when only bodies can be long? But the virtue that is called greatness of mind is rightly understood as referring not to any extent of space, but to a certain force, that is, to the power and capacity of the mind;
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (cam for cum, inlerpretari for interpretari, virr tutes for virtutes, inteNigilnr for intelligitur). "Longanimitas" (literally "long-mindedness") is kept as "longanimity" because the argument turns on the literal sense of "long".

passages.original: Cum vero ea discimus, quoe mirabiliora quam utiliora sunt ; quanquam nonnullis rebus plerumque opportuna, supervacanea tamen et de illo secundo genere numeranda sunt. Non enim si quidam tibicen, ut Varro auctor est, ita populum delectavit ut rex Cieret, idco animum nostrum illo artificio augendum putare dcbemus : quia nec majores quam humani sunt, dentes habere vellemus, si audissemus, a quopiam, quod tales habuerit, morsu hostem necatum Noxium vero illud est genus artium, quo animi valcludo sauciatur : nam et odore ac sapore mire dijudicare pulmenta, et quo lacu piscis captus sit, vel quotennc vinum sit, nosse dicere quædam est miscranda peritia ;
passages.english: But when we learn things that are more marvellous than useful, then, although they are often convenient for some purposes, they are nevertheless superfluous and must be counted in that second class. For if a certain flute-player, as Varro reports, so delighted the people that he was made king, we ought not on that account to think that our mind should be enlarged by that skill; for neither would we wish to have teeth larger than human ones, if we had heard from someone that a man who had such teeth killed an enemy with a bite. But that class of arts is harmful by which the health of the mind is wounded: for to judge dishes wonderfully by smell and taste, and to be able to tell in what lake a fish was caught, or how many years old a wine is, is a pitiable sort of expertise;
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently: 'quoe' for 'quae', 'idco' for 'ideo', 'dcbemus' for 'debemus', 'valcludo' for 'valetudo', 'quotennc' for 'quotenne', 'miscranda' for 'miseranda'. 'ut rex Cieret' is evidently corrupt; read as 'ut rex fieret' ('that he was made king'). A sentence break is missing after 'necatum'.

passages.original: Adesto erro huic tanqnam tuæ, ac tuerc illam, dum a me paulisper refellitur. E. Tuebor sane, si tu adjuveris; sin minime, jam mihi displicet : non enin frustra libi visa est refellenda. A. Noli nimis ex auctoritate pendere, praescrtim mea quæ nulla est; et quod ait Horatius, Sapere aude ( Epist. lib. i, epist. 2 v. 39 ) : ne non te ratio subjuget priusquam melus. E. Ego prorsus nihil metuo , quoquo res modo processerit: non enim errarc me sines. Sed jam incipe si quid habes, ne differendo potius quam adversando dcfatiger.
passages.english: Stand by this error as if it were your own, and defend it while I refute it for a little while. E. I will certainly defend it, if you help me; if not, it already displeases me, for it was not without reason that it seemed to you to need refuting. A. Do not depend too much on authority, especially mine, which is none at all. And, as Horace says, "Dare to be wise" (Epistles 1.2.40), so that reason does not subdue you before fear does. E. I fear nothing at all, however the matter turns out, for you will not let me err. But begin now, if you have anything, so that I am not worn out more by your delaying than by your opposing.
passages.notes: "Ne non te ratio subjuget priusquam metus" is awkward; the sense may be "lest fear, rather than reason, subdue you." Scanning errors corrected (erro for errori, tuerc, enin, libi, metus).

passages.original: Vellem hinc plura dicere, ac meipsum constringere, dum quasi tibi praxi. pio, nihil aliud agerem quam redderer mibi, cui uia maxime debeo (iRetract., cap. 8, n. 3) : atque iia Deo fieri, quod ait Horatius, Amicum mancipium do.mine ( Serm. lib. 2. satira 1, v. 2, 3). Qnod omnino fieri non potest, nisi ad ejus reformemur imaginem , quam nobis ut pretiosissimum quiddam et charissimum custodiendam dedit, dum nos ipsos nobis tales dedit , qualibus nibil possit praeter ipsum anteponi.
passages.english: I would like to say more on this point, and to bind myself, so that while I seem, as it were, to be instructing you, I would be doing nothing other than restoring myself to myself, to whom I am most of all indebted (Retractations 1.8.3), and so becoming to God what Horace speaks of, "a slave dear to his master" (Satires 2.7.2–3). This cannot happen at all unless we are re-formed to his image, which he gave us to guard as something most precious and most dear, when he gave us to ourselves as beings such that nothing except himself could be preferred to them.
passages.notes: "Praxi. pio" read as praecipio ("instruct"). The text has "cui uia maxime debeo"; it is read as "cui maxime debeo", and the stray "uia" is unclear. The Horace reference given (Serm. 2, sat. 1) seems to be wrong; the quoted line comes from Satires 2.7.
